hero.headline: Two teens fired at each other in Indian River County shootout, deputies say
hero.teaser: Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incide
hero.body:
Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire.

 Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. Kevin Jaworski, a spokesman for the sheriff's office, confirmed the exchange. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting.

 Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. The weapon was described as a short-barreled pistol rifle.

 Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. Jaworski said the shooting was between the two juveniles and there is no threat to the community at this point, but noted it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because a car was hit and a house was hit, and anyone in those locations could have easily been hurt.

 Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives.

cards.headline: Vero Beach police expect more charges, additional victims in AI deepfake sexual images case
cards.teaser: Police say more charges are expected against Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, who was arrested Wednesday and held on $1 million bond, and investigators believe several additional victims have yet to be identified.
cards.body:
A Vero Beach man arrested Wednesday on eight charges for creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent is expected to face additional charges as investigators believe more victims have yet to be identified. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond after his arrest on charges stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 involving one adult female victim. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared.

 Ruma faces three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. The victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma's home and seized two phones, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation.

 Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women, including images from social media and other publicly available online sources, to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said.

 Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police also said the investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years.

 Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.

cards.headline: DeSantis pledges to campaign for Amendment 3 as local leaders warn of service cuts and fee hikes
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school proper
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Under the amendment's ballot language, the expanded exemption would not apply to school district taxes.

 The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including businesses and rental properties, from 10 percent to 5 percent, and restrict how counties and municipalities use property-tax revenue. DeSantis said he has not settled on how he will participate and would not lead a political committee's statewide fundraising effort, but added he would be involved because he thinks the amendment is important.

 The governor rejected warnings from local leaders that the amendment would leave communities unable to provide basic services. DeSantis said he would support state funding to help rural counties with limited tax bases absorb revenue losses, though any state assistance would depend on lawmakers approving the funding. Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava launched a South Florida campaign Wednesday to defeat Amendment 3, joined by local leaders, labor organizations and business and civic groups. She warned that communities could face service cuts, higher fees or some combination of both, and said Miami-Dade could lose about 10 percent of its general fund revenue in the first year and 20 percent in the second.

 Levine Cava said renters and businesses could shoulder additional costs without receiving the expanded homestead exemption. Supporters have potentially encouraging polling numbers. A Sachs Media survey conducted August 18 randomly assigned 800 Florida voters to groups reviewing either the original ballot language or a court-ordered revision.

 Support was 65 percent among those who read the revised wording, compared with 60 percent among those who saw the original. The difference was not statistically significant.

 The Florida Policy Institute estimates that public hospital districts and health systems would lose approximately $323 million over three years under Amendment 3. The institute warns that reduced funding could affect staffing, access to care and programs serving uninsured and underinsured patients. Amendment 3 requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters casting ballots on the measure in November. If approved, it would take effect in January.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman among 7 charged in alleged $57M IRS tax refund fraud scheme
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money.
cards.body:
A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

 Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

cards.headline: Thieves target Florida SNAP recipients, use stolen benefits to buy baby formula at California address
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Florida families reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California, with most purchases for baby formula known to be resold on the black market.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Florida families have reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California. A majority of the purchases are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, the Tampa Bay 28 I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula.

 Victims described the financial toll of the theft. Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team that she and her family still have not had all of their bills covered because of the theft. Cheyanne Smith said she has gone through three cards and that locks, canceling the card and changing her PIN have not worked.

 In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing that they had delivered formula there like two or three times and each time it was like five to seven cans.

 The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues. The Department of Children and Families has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts.

 Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud, meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned.

cards.headline: Indiantown council fires village manager Taryn Kryzda, names former Stuart city manager as interim
cards.teaser: The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda and appointed Michael Giardino, who was recently fired as Stuart city manager, as interim village manager during a contentious meeting that also addressed data center development.
cards.body:
The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had been in the role since 2023, and appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager during a meeting originally called to discuss a moratorium on data centers. Giardino was recently fired as Stuart city manager. The council also voted 4-1 to reject a proposed temporary pause on new large-scale data center applications and will instead seek a new legal opinion and lawsuit-proof language before taking action.

 Giardino said he was approached by two council members about the position and attended the special meeting where the council made its decision. He said it appeared to him that the voters wanted a change in Indiantown and that the village council received that information.

 Kimberly Jackson Brown, a 59-year resident of Indiantown, said the decision was a step in the right direction because the biggest change has to be to have the trust of the people for the council. She said if the village has a council that residents can trust, then all the changes can be enacted.

 The meeting addressed data centers, which has sparked debate within the community. After hearing public input, the council rejected a resolution to pause data center development and instructed its new legal counsel to revise the proposal's language. The data center issue will return to the council for further discussion.

cards.headline: Woman facing 72 charges in Palm City dog hoarding case pleads not guilty after surrendering animals
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered by O'Donnell, clearing the way for adoptions. According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions.

The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said staff shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher said some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur.

hero.headline: DeSantis pledges to campaign for Amendment 3 as local leaders warn of service cuts and fee hikes
hero.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school proper
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Under the amendment's ballot language, the expanded exemption would not apply to school district taxes.

 The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including businesses and rental properties, from 10 percent to 5 percent, and restrict how counties and municipalities use property-tax revenue. DeSantis said he has not settled on how he will participate and would not lead a political committee's statewide fundraising effort, but added he would be involved because he thinks the amendment is important.

 The governor rejected warnings from local leaders that the amendment would leave communities unable to provide basic services. DeSantis said he would support state funding to help rural counties with limited tax bases absorb revenue losses, though any state assistance would depend on lawmakers approving the funding. Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava launched a South Florida campaign Wednesday to defeat Amendment 3, joined by local leaders, labor organizations and business and civic groups. She warned that communities could face service cuts, higher fees or some combination of both, and said Miami-Dade could lose about 10 percent of its general fund revenue in the first year and 20 percent in the second.

 Levine Cava said renters and businesses could shoulder additional costs without receiving the expanded homestead exemption. Supporters have potentially encouraging polling numbers. A Sachs Media survey conducted August 18 randomly assigned 800 Florida voters to groups reviewing either the original ballot language or a court-ordered revision.

 Support was 65 percent among those who read the revised wording, compared with 60 percent among those who saw the original. The difference was not statistically significant.

 The Florida Policy Institute estimates that public hospital districts and health systems would lose approximately $323 million over three years under Amendment 3. The institute warns that reduced funding could affect staffing, access to care and programs serving uninsured and underinsured patients. Amendment 3 requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters casting ballots on the measure in November. If approved, it would take effect in January.

cards.headline: Thieves target Florida SNAP recipients, use stolen benefits to buy baby formula at California address
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Florida families reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California, with most purchases for baby formula known to be resold on the black market.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Florida families have reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California. A majority of the purchases are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, the Tampa Bay 28 I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula.

 Victims described the financial toll of the theft. Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team that she and her family still have not had all of their bills covered because of the theft. Cheyanne Smith said she has gone through three cards and that locks, canceling the card and changing her PIN have not worked.

 In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing that they had delivered formula there like two or three times and each time it was like five to seven cans.

 The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues. The Department of Children and Families has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts.

 Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud, meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned.

cards.headline: Indiantown council fires village manager Taryn Kryzda, names former Stuart city manager as interim
cards.teaser: The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda and appointed Michael Giardino, who was recently fired as Stuart city manager, as interim village manager during a contentious meeting that also addressed data center development.
cards.body:
The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had been in the role since 2023, and appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager during a meeting originally called to discuss a moratorium on data centers. Giardino was recently fired as Stuart city manager. The council also voted 4-1 to reject a proposed temporary pause on new large-scale data center applications and will instead seek a new legal opinion and lawsuit-proof language before taking action.

 Giardino said he was approached by two council members about the position and attended the special meeting where the council made its decision. He said it appeared to him that the voters wanted a change in Indiantown and that the village council received that information.

 Kimberly Jackson Brown, a 59-year resident of Indiantown, said the decision was a step in the right direction because the biggest change has to be to have the trust of the people for the council. She said if the village has a council that residents can trust, then all the changes can be enacted.

 The meeting addressed data centers, which has sparked debate within the community. After hearing public input, the council rejected a resolution to pause data center development and instructed its new legal counsel to revise the proposal's language. The data center issue will return to the council for further discussion.

cards.headline: Palm City woman pleads not guilty to 72 charges in Border Collie hoarding case, surrenders dogs for adoption
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from the rescue of 36 Border Collies from her Palm City home earlier this month and legally surrendered the dogs for adopt
cards.body:
Paige O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from the rescue of 36 Border Collies from her Palm City home earlier this month and legally surrendered the dogs for adoption. Martin County court records show O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls it the worst animal hoarding case in its history.

 The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's home on Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood.

 The rescued Border Collies underwent medical grooming, a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said staff shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, investigators found lots of pieces of metal, rusted metal, sharp metal that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass, according to Fisher.

 The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay and neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups. The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services.

 The case has prompted State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, to push for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman among 7 charged in alleged $57M IRS tax refund fraud scheme
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money.
cards.body:
A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

 Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

hero.headline: Two teens fired at each other in Indian River County shootout, deputies say
hero.teaser: Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incide
hero.body:
Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire.

 Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. Kevin Jaworski, a spokesman for the sheriff's office, confirmed the exchange. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting.

 Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. The weapon was described as a short-barreled pistol rifle.

 Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. Jaworski said the shooting was between the two juveniles and there is no threat to the community at this point, but noted it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because a car was hit and a house was hit, and anyone in those locations could have easily been hurt.

 Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives.

cards.headline: Vero Beach police expect more charges, additional victims in AI deepfake sexual images case
cards.teaser: Police say more charges are expected against Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, who was arrested Wednesday and held on $1 million bond, and investigators believe several additional victims have yet to be identified.
cards.body:
A Vero Beach man arrested Wednesday on eight charges for creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent is expected to face additional charges as investigators believe more victims have yet to be identified. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond after his arrest on charges stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 involving one adult female victim. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared.

 Ruma faces three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. The victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma's home and seized two phones, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation.

 Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women, including images from social media and other publicly available online sources, to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said.

 Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police also said the investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years.

 Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.
